newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czechs relaunch housing drive at old Soviet base.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czechs relaunch housing drive at old Soviet base.

text.p: "Russians go home" can still be seen, daubed in fading letters on a crumbling stone wall in the sleepy Czech village of Milovice.

The Russians, who once occupied a sprawling military base in Milovice, have been gone for six years. But only now are the homes they occupied after the 1968 invasion of the former Czechoslovakia being reclaimed.

Milovice, a village of around 4,000 people at the end of a railway line 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Prague, is the site of a modest project aimed at helping to reinvigorate the Czech housing programme, which has come close to a halt since the 1989 fall of communism.
Around 100,000 Soviet troops used to live and train at Milovice in a area forbidden to the public and with extensive facilities.

Now the first Czech families are moving into renovated flats abandoned by officers and their families when the Soviet Army left the country in 1991, 23 years after it arrived to crush the "Prague Spring" democratic reform movement.
"This could be a town of 12,000 if everything works out, but it will take a while yet. It won't be tomorrow," says Miloslav Skoch, a construction site supervisor on the project.

Compared with the communists' massive housing developments, Milovice is modest. So far only 29 flats have been refurbished, with another 716 in the pipeline. But Skoch says there are around 4,000 lying empty.
From the 1960s until their demise, the communists ringed Czech cities with rows of grey blocks of flats made from prefabricated concrete panels.
Few people like living on these depressing estates. But they are home for a large percentage of the Czech population and little low-cost housing is now being built.
In communist times, housing was a top priority. Three percent of national income was ploughed into it and more than 44,000 flats were completed in 1989.

This shrunk to just 12,000 in 1995, the lowest since World War Two and the state now spends less than 0.8 percent of gross domestic product on support for housing. Most of what is built now comprises chic villas for the newly-rich and expatriate executives.
DEARTH OF DECENT ACCOMMODATION
This has left a lack of affordable homes and only recently has the government, under pressure after losing a comfortable majority in parliament this year, begun to tackle the problem.

Milovice is an attempt to turn the former military district into an extension of the local town. Since the end of the Cold War, Prague has tried to decide what to do with military areas which were previously marked only as white blobs on the map.
The road to developing Milovice has been beset by red tape. An earlier plan to transform its former military airfield into a local airport was turned down by the government.
Before the flats could be sold off they had to be transferred from the Defence Ministry to a special agency set up to deal with the problem. Then a buyer had to be found.

This process has left them empty for five years, during which they fell into a sorry state. The first flats are now ready and stand next to the village. But the majority, which could form the nucleus of a new Milovice, are in the former prohibited area which begins down a leafy lane.
Behind the now lightly-guarded military checkpoint, a ghost town extends up the hill. Amid dilapidated buildings, a clock stands frozen at 10 o'clock.

Nearby, textbooks in cyrillic script litter the floor of the school built for Russian children. This building, along with a clinic whose heroic socialist mural provides a rare splash of colour, will be handed over to the local authorities.
AREA POLLUTED

The Czech army is still clearing explosives from the area, which was first appropriated by the Austrian imperial army in 1904. The area is also heavily contaminated by oil and aviation fuel, with pollution three metres deep (10 feet) in some areas.
Nevertheless, the site has been declared fit for living.
"The walls of these buildings are sturdy. It will always be cheaper to renovate them," explained Skoch in one block with peeling plasterwork and a stagnant smell.

There could be one snag: what will the new arrivals do for a living? Government literature says new residents "will find work in businesses, in services or in administration, which are branches that it will be necessary to strengthen in connection with an increase in the local population".
The state has pledged to support local enterprises, but Frantisek Selucky of the Ministry for Regional Development says: "It really depends on the people themselves."
Nevertheless, the area, like the country as a whole, does not suffer high unemployment.
If new residents do not want to commute to Prague they could also work in nearby Mlada Boleslav, where the Skoda car plant owned by Germany's Volkswagen is short of staff.
Of course all this need not mean Milovice will be totally turning its back on its sad past.

Aside from decorations inside the village church, in which Russian prisoners left their mark during World War One, there are also plans to restore the oldest barracks and preserve them for their historical value.
But Skoch said: "It will be opened up and it will be an ordinary town" --- for the first time in more than 90 years.
